RAJYA SABHA [10 August, 2001] 
Reduction in production cost of fertilizers 
† *281. SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH 'LALAN'-:†† 
             SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether production cost of fertilizers in the country will go down with 
the announcement of reduction in import duty on Naphtha; 
(b) if so, the names of fertilizers the production cost of which has been 
assessed to go down and by how much; 
(c) whether benefit of this reduction will reach the fertilizer using farmers 
of the country; and 
(d) if so, by when Government ar e likely to announce reduction in 
fertilizer prices? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI 
SUKHDEV SINGH DHINDSA): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on the Table 
of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) As there is no change in the rate of custom duty levied on import 
of Naphtha for manufacture of fertilizers in the current financial year vis-a-
vis the import duty levied on Naphtha during the previous financial year, 
there will not be any change in the cost of production of fertilizers based on 
the consumption of imported Naphtha. 
The selling prices of fertilizers are already far below the cost of production. 
There is no proposal at present to reduce the selling prices of fertilizers.

SHRI KRISHNA KUMAR BIRLA: Mr. Chairman, Sir, I thank you for 
this opportunity. Sir, the Finance Minister in his Budget Speech had 
announced that the Government has decided to implement the 
recommendations of the Expenditure Reforms Commission, ERC, for a 
phased programme of complete de-control of Urea by 2006 and that Unit 
Specific Retention Price Scheme would be replaced by Group Concession 
Scheme as early as possible. ERC had proposed five groups to be constituted. 
The Fertiliser Ministry, I understand, ca rried out this exercise and the result 
was that an awfully distorted picture emerged. It was a case of complete topsy-
turvy. Groups can be formed of units where similar conditions exist. In 
fertiliser industry conditions vary wide ly from unit to unit. To give an 
instance where coal is used to generate  power the cost is low, the cost of 
generation power by gas is very high. And yet in the exercise that the 
Government did, coal units were clubbed with gas units to form a group. It is 
a mistaken belief that the group con cept is a step towards complete de-
control. There is no relationship whatsoever between group concept and de-
control. My question is: What has been the result of the exercise carried out 
by the Government of India in respect of ERC proposals of constituting 
groups, and if the outcome is unsatisfactory, how does the Government 
propose to move in the matter and what are its next steps?

16 

[10 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) whether it has come to the notice of Government that the permission

THE MINISTER FOR ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) Ministry had received two pr oposals in recent past for diversion 
of forest land in favour of Kudremukh Iron Ore Company Limited (KIOCL) 
from the Government of Karnataka under the provisions of Forest 
(Conservation) Act, 1980. 
The first proposal which was received in 1999 relates to renewal of mining 
lease over 4605 hectare of forest land.  The State Government also informed 
that the final notification of Kudremukh National Park was under process. As 
the area proposed for diversion was forming part of Kudremukh National 
Park, the State Government was asked to get a detailed study done on the 
impact of mining on the flora and fauna of the Kudremukh National Park. 
However, keeping in mind that fact that mining was an ongoing activity in 
the area as the first lease was given in 1969, temporary working permission 
was granted for continuation of mining in the already broken up area only as 
an interim measure in July, 1999 for one year which was further extended by 
one year in July, 2000 and by another 3 months in July, 2001. 
The State Government on 14.07.2000 submitted a complementary 
additional proposal for diversion of 30 ha. of forest land in favour of KIOCL 
for the purpose of replacement of the worn out slurry pipeline, which had 
started leaking at certain places. The Ministry considered the proposal in the 
light of the fact that the pipeline is part of the over all operations of KIOCL. 
The Ministry did not approve this proposal in view of the fact that the 
decision for renewal of mining lease of KIOCL was yet to be taken. 
However, keeping in view that temporary working permission had been 
granted to them 
17 

RAJYA SABHA [10 August, 2001] 
for mining, KIOCL was allowed to replace the worn out/leaking slurry 
pipeline on 21.9.2000 in the over all interest of the National Park.

under the provisions of Petroleum and Minerals Pipelines (Acquisition of 
Right of User in Land) Act, 1962 for the purpose of laying slurry pipeline 
from Malleshwara (Kudremukh) to New Mangalore Port at Panambur for 
Kudremukh Iron Ore Company Ltd. vide notification No. S.O. 610(E) dated 
25.10.1978. Therefore the question of the permission under this Act expiring 
in 1980 does not arise. Since the acquisition of the land has been made prior 
to enactment of the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, even clearance under 
Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 is not required for continuation of the 
existing pipeline.

impact of mining on Kudremukh Nationa l Park reveals adverse effect of the 
mining on surrounding areas. The area forms part of the Western Ghats, 
which is very sensitive and fragile  ecosystem. A large number of 
representations have been received against continuation of mining fn the area.

Supreme Court.

† 290. SHRIMATI    SAROJ    DUBEY:    Will    the    Minister    of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state:  
(a) whether Government are aware that pollution in most of the cities 
and towns of the country is increasing day-by-day; 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
34 

[10 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, whether Government have decided to take any time-bound steps 
to check pollution effectively; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T. R. 
BAALU): (a) to (d) An increasing trend of air, water and noise pollution in 
many of the cities and towns of the country has been noticed. To check 
pollution, Government has taken various steps which has resulted in reversal 
of the trend in some of the major cities. Time bound Action Plans were drawn 
up and implemented specially for improving fuel quality, phasing out leaded 
petrol, reduction of benzene in petrol and notifying stricter emission norms. 
The details of the steps taken by the Government to control pollution in 
the country include the following:— 
(1) A comprehensive Policy for Abatement of Pollution that lays stress on 
both the control and preventive aspects of pollution has been 
formulated. 
(2) Effluent and emission standards for industries have been notified under 
the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 to check pollution. 
(3) A network of ambient air (290) and water (507) Quality Monitoring 
Stations covering 90 towns-cities distributed all over the country has 
been set up. Surveys are carried in the major cities from time to time to 
assess the prevailing levels of noise. 
(4) Highly polluting industries have been identified. Defaulting Industries 
have been directed to install necessary pollution control equipment in a 
time bound basis and legal action is taken against the defaulting units. 
(5) For control of water pollution from clusters of small scale indsutries, 
subsidy has been given for 89 Common Effluent Treatment Plants 
(CETPs). 
35 

RAJYA SABHA [10 August, 2001] 
(6) Environment Impact Assessment Notification, 1994 is in force 
governing environmental appraisal of 30 specified categories of 
developmental projects. 
(7) Emission standards for on-road vehicles and mass emission standards 
for new vehicles have been notified under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 
and are enforced by Transport Department of the State Governments. 
(8) Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) is supplied for automobiles through a 
number of retail outlets in Delhi and Mumbai to cater to the CNG fitted 
vehicles. 
(9) Unleaded petrol is supplied in the entire country from 1.2.2000 and 
diesel with 0.25% sulphur maximum content is supplied from 1.1.2000 
in the entire country. Low sulphur (0 .05%) fuel (petrol and diesel) has 
also been introduced in major cities. 
 
(10) A notification to control noise pollution emanating from various sources 
with the help of local authorities has been notified in February, 2000. 
(11) Noise standards for stationary diesel sets (15-500 KVA) have been 
notified in January, 1999. 
(12) Noise standards for fire crackers had been notified in October, 1999. 
(13) Noise limits for portable generator sets run with petrol and kerosene 
have been notified in September, 2000. 
(14) Noise limits for vehicles have been revised and notified in September, 
2000 effective from 1st January, 2003. 
(15) Noise level standards for coal mines have been evolved and notified in 
September, 2000. 
(16) Action Plan for control of pollution in Delhi and Mumbai are being 
implemented and similar action plans have been prepared for Chennai 
and Hyderabad. 
36 

[10 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(17) 24 critically polluted areas have been identified. Action Plan have been 
drawn up for restoration of environmental quality in these areas. 
(18) Environmental epidemiological studies have been initiated in different 
parts of the country to assess the impact of pollution. 
(19) Promotion of environmental education and awareness has been 
launched.

Genetically manipulated BT. Cotton 
2143. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the GM Crop Technology is safe for our environment; and 
(b) if so, the reasons for which the Ministry of Environment has decided to 
postpone commercial clearance of GM crop-transgenic BT. cotton? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) Transgenic crops and other genetically modified organisms hold 
promise for the benefit of mankind through higher production of food material and 
newer medicines. However, concerns have been raised about the potential risks 
which may arise from the release of th ese transgenic organisms. These risks 
include spread of introduced traits to non-target species leading to genetic 
contamination, development of pest and herbicide resistance, contamination of 
food chains, displacement of traditional animal breeds and plant varieties 
thereby causing genetic erosion. 
(b) The Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC) set up under Rule 4 
of the Rules for the Manufacture, Use, Import, Export and Storage of Hazardous 
Micro-organisms/Genetically Engineered Organisms or Cells 1989, considered the 
proposal for release of transgenic BT cotton submitted by Maharashtra Hybrid 
Seeds Company (MAHYCO), at its meeting held on 19.6.2001. The GEAC 
observed that the data generated on large scale field trials on BT. cotton 
undertaken by MAHYCO could not reflect the true values because of late sowing. 
It was decided that the trials be repeated on a larger scale under the direct 
supervision of the Indian Council of Agricultural Research under their Advanced 
Varietal Trials of the All India Coordinated Cotton Improvement Project. In 
addition, GEAC has accorded approval to MAHYCO for conducting field trials on 
farmers' fields in an area of about 100 hectares.

Post harvest management of farm produce 
2150. SHRI S. RAMACHANDRAN PILLAI:  
PROF. (SHRIMATI) BHARATI RAY: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) how Government propose to solve the structural problems including 
fall in prices of agricultural commodities and shortage of godowns for 
storage of surplus foodgrains; and 
(b) what concrete steps are being taken by Government on post harvest 
management of farm produce? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) The following steps are taken by the 
Government to solve the problem of fall in prices of agricultural 
commodities and oi shortage of storage space: 
Government announces, each season, minimum support prices for major 
agricultural commodities and organizes purchase operations through public 
and cooperative agencies. The designate d agencies intervene in the market 
and undertake procurement operations as  and when the prices fall below the 
minimum support price fixed by the Government. 
When prices of horticultural commodities of importance fall below the 
economic levels, the Government of India, at the request of State 
Governments, launches Market intervention Scheme for that particular 
commodity and in that particular season to prevent distress sale by farmers. 
The government has form ulated a National Storage Policy aimed at 
harnessing the resources of the public and private sector for augmentation of 
infrastructure to handle foodgrains including construction of bulk storage 
facilities and also conventional godowns. The total storage capacity available 
with different public and cooperative sector agencies is 925.71 lakh M.T. 
For the creation of new storage capac ity, the following further steps are 
being taken: 
87 

RAJYA SABHA [10 August, 2001] 
(i) Creation of additional storage capacity (estimated at 54 lakh 
Tonnes) by state Governments, SWC and CWC on the basis of 
long-term guarantee by FCI. 
(ii) Creation of 21 lakh tones capacity for bulk handling, storage and 
transportation facilities through private sector participation at 11 
locations. 
(iii) Creation of conventional godowns totaling 5.88 lakh tones through 
private sector participation at 54 locations in 14 States. 
(b) In order to reduce losses to foodgrains during the post-harvest period, 
the Government of India is implementing the Save Grain Campaign Scheme. 
The main thrust of this scheme is on training, demonstration and publicity in 
the field of scientific storage of foodgrains at the farm level. Improvement of 
grains storage structures, popularization of scientific storage structures and 
other activities are also carried out under the save Grain Campaign for the 
benefit of farmers. 
The National Horticulture Board (NHB), is implementing the following 
schemes for strengthening the post-harvest management infrastructure for 
horticultural produce:— 
(i) Capital Investment Subsidy for construction/expansion/ 
modernization of Cold Storages/Storages for horticulture produce; 
(ii) Development of commercial horticulture through production and 
post harvest management of horticultural products. 
These schemes would, inter-alia, help in checking losses in weight and 
quality of agricultural and horticultural produce and thereby ensure benefits 
to farmers.

Noise pollution in Delhi 
2164. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that 25 per cent  of residential colonies of Delhi 
have excessive levels of noise all the day and the noise level is set to rise in 
the coming years; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that many cases of children with partial hearing 
loss due to vehicular noise pollution have been received in AI IMS and 
children are very sensitive to noise and, as a result, get harmed more easily; 
and 
(c) if so, what steps are being taken to check the noise pollution? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) According to a study conducted by Delhi Pollution Control 
Committee in 1996, in 14 out of 46 residential colonies noise levels were 
found to be exceeding the prescribed standards. 
(b) According to All India Institute of Medical Sciences, cases of children 
and adults with noise related hearing loss have been seen and that major 
cause of hearing loss in children is infection of noise, sinus extending into the 
ear. 
105 

RAJYA SABHA [10 August, 2001] 
(c) The Government have taken various steps to check noise pollution, 
which include the following: 
(1) Ambient Air Quality Standards in respect of noise have been notified in 
1989 under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 for the i ndustrial, 
commercial, residential areas and silence zones. 
(2) Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 have been 
notified in February, 2000. 
(3) Noise standards for st ationary diesel sets  (15-500KVA) have been 
notified in January, 1999. 
(4) Noise standards for fire crackers had been notified in October, 1999. 
(5) Noise limits for portable generator sets run with petrol and kerosene have 
been notified in September, 2000. 
(6) Noise limits for vehicles have been revised and notified in September, 
2000 effective from 1st January, 2003. 
(7) Noise level standards for coal mines have been evolved and notified in 
September, 2000. 
Death of rhinos at Delhi Zoo 
2165.  SHRI CM. IBRAHIM:  
DR. KARAN SINGH: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that two rhinos died at Delhi Zoo in April this year 
and more were suffering acutely; if so , the reasons for spread of the deadly 
disease; 
(b) whether a number of Rhinos have died or have been killed in different Zoos 
and sanctuaries during 1999-2000, 2000-2001 and in 2001, till date; if so, the 
details thereof; and 
(c) the steps taken to preserve and promote this endangered specie? 
 
 
106 

[10 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) Two rhinos have died in Delhi Zoo on 24-4-2001 and 25-4-2001. 
Rest of the two rhinos are hale and hearty. 
(b) The number of Rhinos poached, killed and died natural death in national 
parks and sanctuaries during the years 1999, 2000 and 2001 (till April) is 70, 68 
and 2 respectively. 2 Rhinos have died each year during 1999-2000, 2000-2001 
and in 2001 (till date) in zoos. 
(c) The Steps taken by the Government to protect Rhinoceros are as follows: 
 
(1) Extensive patrolling is done by the protection staff in all national 
parks and sanctuaries forming part of rhino habitat. 
(2) 100% financial assistance is provided by the Central Government both 
for non-recurring and recurring items of expenditure including the 
incremental staff. 
(3) Rhino is placed in Schedule I of Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 
thereby getting the highest level of protection. Trading in rhino parts and 
products is also banned by law. 
(4) Cooperation of Police, BSF, DRI and Army is taken, as and when 
required, in apprehending the poachers and illegal traders. 
(5) India is a party to the Convention on International Trade in Endangered 
Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) and abides by the regulations 
of international trade in endangered species of animals and articles. Under 
the provisions of the Convention, rhino is covered under Appendix I of 
CITES, which bans international trade in the species, products and 
derivatives. 
(6) Regional and sub-regional offices on wildlife preservation are functioning 
at the main export centres of th e country to prevent smuggling of 
wildlife products.

harvesting, pasture development, promotion of horticulture and agro-forestry,

Population of Sarus Crane 
2170. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the population of Sarus Crane, the tallest of the flying birds, in 
Gujarat; 
(b) what is their population in the State as a percentage of world population; 
(c) whether their population is fast dwindling, as per various census 
report; 
(d) whether the bird is listed as endangered specie in the schedule of Wildlife 
Protection Act, 1972; and 
(e) if not, whether Government are making any review to change the 
schedule? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) As per the latest survey carried out in 2001 by Gujarat 
Ecological Education Research Foundation, Gandhinagar, the estimated number 
of Sarus Cranes in the State is about 1403. Estimated number of Indian Sarus Cranes 
in the world is about 8000-10000. Thus existing Sarus Crane population in Gujarat is 
about 15.5% of the world population. 
(c) There has been a decline over the years in the population of 
Sarus Cranes. 
(d) Sarus Crane is listed under Schedule IV of the Wildlife 
(Protection) Act, 1972. 
(e) As the species enjoys protection against hunting all over the 
country, there is no need to transfer it to any other Schedule.

Dumping grounds for toxic products 
2179. SHRI KRISHNA KUMAR BIRLA: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that while the world is getting rid of the toxic 
products, Government are promoting the waste incineration through special 
subsidies and the country is fast becoming the dumping ground for the 
world's most toxic products; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that while the world over chemicals have been 
banned, these are being still used in the country; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the measures taken by Government to prevent the country from 
becoming a dumping grounds for toxic products? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) There are no subsidies for promoting incineration of toxic wastes in 
the country. In respect of energy recovery from municipal solid wastes and 
industrial wastes, there is a scheme under the Ministry of Non-conventional Energy 
Sources (MNES) of the Government of India, which provides for subsidy on 
term loan to reduce the interest rate to 7.5% subject to a ceiling per megawatt of 
electricity generated of Rs. 2.00 crores in respect of urban waste projects and 
Rs. 1.50 crores in respect of Industrial waste projects. This scheme applies to all 
municipal solid wastes and industrial wastes conversion    technologies    such    as   
biomethanation,    pelletisation, 
122 

[10 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
gassification, pyrolysis including incineration. MNES also has a scheme 
providing for capital subsidy upto 50% of capital cost subject to a maximum 
of Rs. 3.00 crores per megawatt of energy produced for setting up 
Demonstration Projects, one in each Stat e, for various waste processing and 
treatment technologies. 
(b) and (c) The Ministry of Environment and Forests, Government of 
India, assigned the preparation of a "S tate of the Art Report on chemicals 
and products whose production and import/export have been banned by other 
countries but continue to be produced and used in India" to the National 
Institute of Science, Technology and Development Studies (NISTADS), New 
Delhi. NISTADS has submitted the draft final report to the Ministry of 
Environment and Forests on 23rd July, 2001. The manufacture, use and 
import and export of toxic chemicals is regularly reviewed by the Ministry of 
Agriculture, Ministry of Health and Ministry of Environment and Forests 
and decision to phase out toxic products is taken keeping in view their 
benefits and potential risks to human health and environment. 
(d) The Ministry of Environment and Forests has taken following steps to 
prevent the country from becoming a dumping ground for toxic products: 
(i)  Benzidine and benzidine based dyes (47 numbers) have been banned 
since 1993. 
(ii)  Azodyes (70 numbers) have been banned since 1997. 
(iii)  Hazardous wastes containing ar senic, cyanide, mercury, beryllium, 
selenium, chromium (hexavalent), thallium, pesticides, herbicides, 
insecticides, PCB, PCT, etc. have been banned since 1997. 
(iv)  Under the In sect ids Act, 1968, Ministry of Agriculture has banned 
or restricted nearly 30 pesticides. Some of these are included in the 
Stockholm Convention dealing with persistent organic pollutants. The 
Ministry of Health has also banned a number of food additives under 
the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.

2196. DR. DASARI NARAYANA RAO:  Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:

in Primary and Upper primary schools in the country under Sarva Shiksha 
Abhiyan (SSA);

MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) and (b) Under Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan it is 
proposed to provide a room for every teacher in primary and upper primary 
schools, with the provision that there would be two class rooms with a 
verandah for every primary school with at least two teachers.

Abhiyan for carrying out pre-project activities in four districts in Andhra 
Pradesh viz. East Godavari, Hyderabad, Krishna and West Godavari. Other 
districts of Andhra Pradesh arc covered under the District Primary Education 
Programme. After completion of pre-project activities, the State Government 
has submitted District Elementary Education Plans for these Districts which 
have been appraised. The plans fr om Andhra Pradesh would be placed 
before the Project Approval Board for consideration and sanction, of grants.

2215. SHRI K.M. SAIFULLAH: Will the Minister of HUMAN

2243. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of 
RAILWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of cases of compassionate appointments pending in the 
South-Central Railway for more than two years; 
(b) whether Government are aware of  the Supreme Court ruling that 
compassionate appointments should not be made in ordinary cases and these 
should be made only on exceptional grounds; 
(c) if so, what are those grounds and how the Ministry is dealing with this 
subject; and 
(d) the steps taken to clear th e long pending compassionate 
appointment cases? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL): 
(a) There are 202 cases of compassionate appointments pending for more 
than two years, as on 30.06.2001, in the South Central Railway; 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) Hon'ble Supreme Court in their judg ement have made it clear that, as 
a rule, appointments in the public services should be made strictly on the 
basis of open invitation of applications and merit. However, there are some 
exceptions to this general rule carved out in the interests of justice. One such 
exception is in favour of the dependents of an employee dying in harness and 
leaving his family in penury and without any means of livelihood. The whole 
object of granting compassionate appointment is thus to enable the family to 
tide over the sudden crisis. These ru lings of Hon'ble Supreme Court have 
been circulated to all Zonal Railw ays-Production Units for guidance. 
However, unlike other MinistriesDepartments, Ministry of Railways is an 
operating organisation employing huge manpower. Consequently, the number 
of compassionate appointments to be given are also correspondingly large. 
Compassionate appointment cases are, therefore, considered on the merits of 
each case.

Genetically engineered rice 
2255. PROF. A. LAKSHMISAGAR: Will the Minister of 
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to develop and introduce genetically 
engineered rice (Golden Rice) when other countries and international 
organisations are against the entry of genetically modified foods; and 
(b) if so, what are the reasons for opting for genetically modified 
189 

RAJYA SABHA [10 August, 2001] 
rice when introduction of genetically modified food is opposed by several 
countries and by experts? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI BACHI SINGH RAWAT): (a) and (b) The 
Department of Biotechnology in collaboration with Indian Council of Agricultural 
Research (ICAR) is working at present on a Joint Research proposal on Golden 
Rice under the second phase of Indo-Swiss Collaboration in Biotechnology. In spite 
of resistance to genetically modified crops by some countries, genetically 
engineered crops have been cultivated in about 46.9 million hectares during the 
year 2000 all over the world. Developing countries like Argentina, China, South 
Africa, Romania, Mexico, Bulgaria, Portugal, Ukraine and Uruguay have almost 
11 million hectares under transgenic crop cultivation. Public concerns regarding the 
safety of environment and consumers are addressed globally through stringent 
national regulatory frameworks. 
Recent National Nutrition Monitoring Bureau (NNMB) repeat survey has 
indicated the prevalence of deficiency of vitamin-A in 0.7% of pre-school 
children. Accordingly, it is estimated that about 12 million people may be 
suffering from vitamin-A deficiency. Traditional breeding methods have been 
unsuccessful in producing crops containing high vitamin-A content. Further, 
existing vitamin-A supplementation programmes are expensive and complicated. 
Development of vitamin-A rich rice varieties to address nutritional requirements is 
one of the sustainable solutions, taking note of all bio-safety requirements. This 
rice would be introduced only after successfully completing all trials following 
the national regulations.

SHRI KAPIL SIBAL (Bihar): With your  permission, Sir, I would like to 
raise an issue with respect to the statement made by the hon. Finance 
Minister, Shri Yashwant Sinha, in this  House during the course of discussion 
on the UTI issue. As you know, Sir, durin g the course of that discussion, the 
Members of this House, especially on this side, raised issues regarding the 
fact that the hon. Finance Minister was informed by the ex-Chairman of the 
UTI, Shri Subramanyam, as to the state of affairs of the UTI. The hon. Minister 
responded to it and accepted that, in fact, two letters were written on the 18 th 
May and 30th June, but said that no demand was made by the ex-Chairman of 
the UTI and nothing really relevant was st ated in those letters. In response to 
the other questions raised by Members of this House, as to what happened on 
the 2 nd July, the Minister stated that on the 30 lh June, when the letter was 
received by the Finance Ministry, he  was informed about it only on the 
morning of the 2nd July. He admitted that he met Shri Subramanyam, but then 
he stated that as far as the decision as  to what was to happen to the US-64, 
that was left to the Board of Trustees of  the UTI, and that he intervened in the 
matter only after the Board of Trustees  took a decision. I am afraid, Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, and I should say this with consternation that in a news report 
published in the Business Standard on the 4 Ih August, there is a quotation

PROF. M.M. AGARWAL (Uttar Prades h): Hon. Chairman, Sir, I 
would like to draw your attention to the fact that Hinda lco and Nalco are the 
world's lowest-cost producers of alumin ium, but their selling prices are the

high import duty imposed on aluminium. Th e cost of production of Hindalco is

metric tonne. Although aluminium is bei ng sold all over the world at LME 
price, i.e. Rs.67,000 per metric t onne; in India, the selling price has 
deliberately been kept very high, at Rs.83,000 per metric tonne.

very high. The landed cost of imported metal in India is approximately 
Rs.91,500 per metric tonne, including import duty. The indigenous primary 
producers are selling their metal at Rs.83,000 per metric tonne.

low. In Thailand, it is one per cent; in Bangladesh, it is five per cent; in 
Pakistan, it is 10 per cent; in Indonesia, it  is nil; whereas in India, it is 30.8 per 
cent. As per the WTO agreement also, I ndia must reduce the import duty and 
keep it at the maximum, i.e. at five  per cent. Because of high prices, the 
consumption of aluminium is coming down  and it is leading to consumption of 
other materials elsewhere. If the pric e is reasonable, the consumption of

reduce the import duty on aluminium me tal, which will automatically bring

no problem for operating passenger/cargo ships for those countries.

modernisation of this port at the earliest.

SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN (Kerala): Hon. Chairman, Sir, the 
Communist Party of India, which I represent, had welcomed the initiative taken 
by the Prime Minister of India to invite Mr. Musharraf, the President of Pakistan 
for Summit-level talks. It is so because we believed that the disputes between 
the countries will have to be settled through negotiations. Resorting to the 
tactics of settling the disputes through force will be very dangerous and 
disastrous. That is why we had supported that initiative. Sir, at the same time, 
we thought that the Government mi ght have done some preparations before 
the start of the Summit. The Summit-level talks between the Heads of States 
is quite different from the talks at the offi cial level, at the level of Secretaries or 
even at the Ministerial level. It being so , Sir, a carefu.l and serious preparation 
will have to be made, while we arrang e for Summit-level ta lks. At several 
levels, discussions should have been carrie d on, at the official level, at the 
Ministerial level, etc. just to explore or probe the mind of the other party, to 
understand what perspective they are having and also to understand whether 
there is any amount of agree ment that could be reached. But, to my surprise, 
the Government has failed in that. It was a very serious mistake on the part of 
the Government of not having done su ch a serious preparation. Now, the 
Summit had ended, and we could neither arrive at a minimum settlement, nor 
we could come out with a joint declarati on. Even then we are of the view that 
we will have to continue the dialogue.  There is no other way to solve the 
problems between the two countries. 
At the same time, I would like to point out that the Prime Minister had 
stated: "We made progress despite differe nces in our perspectives. We made 
progress towards bridging the approaches in the draft joint document." So, if 
you go through what he said in his statement, you will find that both the parties 
were having different perspectives. While Gen. Musharraf was asking to focus 
on Kashmir and had even gone to the extent of stating that without Kashmir no 
other issue could be discussed, the Govern ment  of  India  was  taking  the  
position  that  we  should   have  a

made as extensive a statement on behalf of the Government, as I could

Patel mentioned in one sentence, "A friendly Pakistan would be amalgamated; 
a hostile Pakistan should be eliminated". That silenced Mohammad Ali Jinnah. 
When Liaquat Ali came to power, he showed clenched fists to India -- a 
symbol of hostility. Nehru responded with sending the Army to the frontier. 
When Liaquat protested, what was Nehr u's answer? He said, "You show us 
clenched fists. Are we going to respond with a handshake? We will respond 
with bayonets". He stopped. Ayub Khan misadventured in the Rann of Kachh. 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI SURESH PACHOURI): Please 
conclude now. 
DR. M. N. DAS: Shastriji taught a lesson. Now, I give these examples 
for one reason. If you want to have further dialogue with Pakistan, talk in terms 
of strength, talk as the representative head of the largest democratic nation. 
Do not go for dialogue as a sub-State; go  as a strong State, as a super-State, 
as a tough State. That is my humble request. I am sure -- my good friend Shri 
Sharief-uddin and Hon'ble Shri Omar Abdulla are here - Kashmiriyat will 
continue. One nation t heory will continue in India, as  long as India exists and 
Kashmir exists. Pakistan can never dream of getting Kashmir, even an inch of 
Kashmir. I have no time to show what the Indian Independence Act said. What 
did it contain? What did it define? It said  that those parts which seceded from 
the Indian mainland, formed Pakistan; rest of the historical India remained as 
India. The historical entit y of India is not touched thereby; only those parts 
which seceded formed Pakistan. So. Kashmir did not secede. The historic 
India contained Kashmir and the rest of  India. So, India remained eternal 
India. Pakistan disintegrated within 25 years. Zulfikar Ali Bhutto might have 
declared a thousand year war against India, but his Army ultimately hanged 
him. So, Kashmir is not our problem. It is not our dispute with Pakistan. We 
want friendship with the Pakistani people, but not at the cost of honour, dignity 
and prestige of India.
